A subsequent EO 14389 (Feb-2026) also struck down some IEEPA duties; a US Court of International Trade ruling separately invalidated the Section 122 surcharge. Net effect for Ecuadorian coffee as of the Aug-2026 access date: 0% duty, no surcharge -- but this is the product of a fast-moving, still-finalizing policy situation, not a settled multi-year FTA; VERIFY CURRENT STATUS closer to submission. On the compliance side: FDA Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP) + mandatory Prior Notice filing + FDA food-facility registration apply to all coffee imports (unrelated to tariffs, these are food-safety non-tariff requirements under FSMA).

non_tariff_notes: CRITICAL, VERY RECENT CAVEAT: despite the CAN 0% baseline, Ecuador and Colombia fought an active bilateral tariff war from Feb-2026 to Jun-2026. Ecuador (Pres. Noboa) imposed a 'tasa de seguridad' on Colombian imports starting 21-Jan-2026 (citing insufficient anti-narcotics cooperation), escalating 30%(1-Mar)->50%->100%(1-May-2026). Colombia (Pres. Petro) retaliated via Decreto 0170 (30-Apr-2026), imposing tiered tariffs of 30%/35%/50%/75% on 191 Ecuadorian products EXPLICITLY INCLUDING COFFEE (cafe), plus rice, beans, plantain, sugar. The Comunidad Andina's own Secretariat/Tribunal ruled (7-May-2026) that both measures violated the Cartagena Agreement and ordered both countries to remove them within 10 days; Ecuador initially refused compliance (appealed), but ultimately Ecuador revoked its measures effective 1-Jun-2026, and Colombia's tariffs on Ecuadorian goods came down around the same time (a residual Colombian land-border restriction on rice persisted to ~15-Jul-2026 for unrelated reasons). Sources describe a return to normal trade conditions expected by Jul/Aug-2026. TAKEAWAY FOR THE REPORT: the 'permanent' 0% CAN preference for coffee is not immune to sudden unilateral suspension by either government even without formally exiting CAN -- a real, recent (2026) globalization/regional-integration fragility example worth citing.
